entities.name: University of Pennsylvania
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The University of Pennsylvania (Penn), founded 1740 by Benjamin Franklin as the College of Philadelphia — the first American university explicitly designed for practical education (law, medicine, business, the arts and sciences) rather than training Protestant clergy — is the founding institution of the Wharton School (1881, the world's first business school) and the Penn Medicine system (among the world's largest academic medical centers), as well as the site of ENIAC (1945), the first general-purpose electronic computer. Penn's charter commitment to secular, practical education shaped the American university model.

Franklin's 1749 Proposals Relating to the Education of Youth in Pennsylvania explicitly rejected the classical/clerical curriculum — Greek, Latin, theology — in favor of English composition, history, natural philosophy, mathematics, and practical arts. Penn was the first American university to appoint a professor of medicine (1765), creating the first American medical school. The Wharton School (1881), founded by industrialist Joseph Wharton, created the academic field of business administration — graduate business education, MBA programs globally, trace their lineage to Wharton's model.

ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer), built 1943-1945 at Penn by engineers John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert, was the first general-purpose electronic computer — 30 tons, 1,500 square feet, 18,000 vacuum tubes, capable of 5,000 additions per second. ENIAC's demonstration in 1946 launched the computing age. Penn's hospital system (Penn Medicine) operates 6 hospitals and 1,600 physicians, making it one of the world's largest academic medical systems.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Penn is where three revolutions in American civilization converged: Franklin's secular practical university model, the Wharton School's creation of business education, and ENIAC's invention of the general-purpose computer — making Penn's campus the birthplace of both business schools and the computing age.
